source.title: An Information Theoretic Perspective on Agentic System Design
source.authors: Shizhe He; A. Narayan; Ishan S. Khare; Scott W. Linderman; Christopher Ré; Dan Biderman

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether downstream accuracy or perplexity changes with model scale, but in compressor-predictor systems at inference time rather than by measuring language-model pretraining loss or fitting the original pretraining scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports compressor-size sweeps and their downstream accuracy/perplexity outcomes, which bear on V6. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws for loss, test extrapolation from smaller pretraining runs, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Its mutual-information and bit-efficiency measurements are not outcomes named by the claim versions; they are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It swaps off-the-shelf instruct checkpoints of different sizes as the compressor in a two-model pipeline and reports how pipeline task accuracy or perplexity changes. The checkpoints differ in training data and recipe and come from different families, so this is not a scale sweep of language models. No curve is fitted to size, compute or pretraining loss, and no prediction is checked against held-out scales. The phrase 'scaling laws' is used informally. Pipeline performance as a function of one component's size is a related but different construct from V6, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that compressor quality dominates: the importance ranking is compressor family > compressor size > predictor size. Scaling compressors beats scaling predictors and costs sublinear FLOPs because larger compressors are more concise. Mutual information rate between context and compression is a task-agnostic proxy that correlates with accuracy and perplexity. They make no claim about pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: This study scales instruction-tuned compressors and predictors in inference-time compression-prediction systems and measures downstream task results; it does not use the original sources' pretraining-loss sweeps or compute-optimal training allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by component and dataset: compressor scaling is reported as more effective than predictor scaling, and predictor gains from 70B to 405B differ between LongHealth and FinanceBench. Compressor-family scaling behavior also differs in the paper's results.

fits_no_version.finding: In compressor-predictor pipelines, larger off-the-shelf compressor checkpoints raise task accuracy and lower evaluator perplexity across five datasets and three families. Predictor scaling from 70B to 405B saturates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compound LM system performance rises with compressor component size more than with predictor size.

fits_no_version.finding: The pipeline matches or beats single-frontier-model baselines at lower API cost.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Local compressors can recover frontier-model accuracy at a fraction of the cost.

record.problems: The reported text gives few exact downstream metric values for size sweeps; many results are qualitative statements or figure-based. Some reported comparisons are maxima or aggregates across model families. The study evaluates inference-time compressor-predictor systems, not pretraining loss or extrapolation from fitted power laws.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying V6 outcomes were extracted from figure-only plots where the text did not state a value or explicit outcome. Mutual-information and bit-efficiency results were excluded because those measures are not named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss or power-law fit.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime.
No controlled single-model scale sweep, no fit to size or loss, and no predictive check. Only monotone trends across mixed off-the-shelf checkpoints in a pipeline.
No examination of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label is dropped. The size axis mixes checkpoints with different training tokens and recipes. Several rows (r4, r10, r11) are system-vs-baseline comparisons, not scaling. Evaluator perplexity (Llama-3.1-8B) is not the scaled model's loss.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or tests predicting much larger pretraining runs.
No fixed-pretraining-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token trends.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
No test of the claimed pretraining-loss power-law form across modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

Tests downstream results across compressor/predictor sizes in compressor-predictor tasks; does not test prediction from pretraining loss or quantify out-of-sample forecasts from a fitted scaling curve.
Does not examine pretraining-law exponents or compute-optimal splits under alternative parameter counts, schedules, data, or fitting methods.

rows.subject: Qwen-2.5 compressor
rows.operation_detail: Scaled compressor size and measured downstream LongHealth QA accuracy.
rows.value: Accuracy improves by 60% when scaling from 1B to 7B.
rows.note: The paper reports this as a size-scaling result for the compressor-predictor system, not as a pretraining-loss result.
rows.check: Measures compound-system accuracy against compressor checkpoint size, not LM downstream scaling. No fitted or predictive relation. The abstract's 7B vs 1.5B Qwen figure (1.6× more accurate) differs from this 60% claim.

rows.subject: Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and Gemma-3 compressors
rows.size_stated: Largest model of each family compared with 1B model sizes
rows.stage_stated: instruction-tuned compressors; used to construct chat memories
rows.operation_detail: Scaled compressor size and measured downstream perplexity on synthetic memory questions.
rows.measure: Perplexity (the prose also describes the comparison as lower log probabilities)
rows.value: Larger compressors yield lower perplexity; the largest compressor of each family yields up to 1.14× lower log probabilities than the 1B model sizes.
rows.note: The text's phrase “lower log probabilities” is retained as stated alongside its explicit lower-perplexity characterization.
rows.check: The perplexity is of a Llama-8B evaluator on answers given compressed memory, not the scaled model's loss. The '1.14× lower log probabilities' wording is ambiguous.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Scaling Llama predictors from 70B to 405B on LongHealth and FinanceBench
reader_labels.reason: The reported accuracy gains are within 12% on LongHealth and within 1% on FinanceBench, indicating that downstream improvement with scale is not uniform across system components or datasets (r5–r6).
